posts.title: Inside Invoke-KqlPS
posts.summary: Why I built a KQL interpreter in PowerShell, what subset it supports today, and how it anchors the rest of the lab.

sections.heading: Why build a local KQL harness at all
paragraphs: The problem was simple: I wanted a place to practice hunting patterns against realistic Sentinel-shaped data without needing a live tenant, ingest budget, or demo workspace every time I wanted to test an idea.

That led to `Invoke-KqlPS.ps1`, a scoped Kusto Query Language interpreter in pure PowerShell. It loads tables from a local SQLite database whose schema mirrors the Microsoft Sentinel / Log Analytics table shapes I care about, keeps rows in memory as PowerShell objects, and treats each tabular operator as a function that takes a table and returns a new table. The pipe stays the mental model all the way through.

The module was never meant to be "all of KQL." The useful target was the subset that shows up constantly in daily SOC work: `where`, `project`, `extend`, `summarize`, `distinct`, `union`, several join kinds, `parse with`, and `mv-expand`, plus the scalar functions you reach for while cleaning data or building pivots.

sections.heading: What the current interpreter actually covers
paragraphs: The supported surface is intentionally honest and written down in the module header. On the tabular side, the interpreter handles:

• `take`, `limit`, `top` • `where` • `project`, `project-keep`, `project-rename`, `project-away` • `extend` • `summarize ... by ...` • `order by` / `sort by` • `distinct` • `union` • `join kind=inner|leftouter|leftanti|innerunique` • `parse with` • `mv-expand` • pass-through handling for `materialize`, `getschema`, and `render`

On the scalar side, it supports the functions I wanted available while teaching or validating hunts: time helpers like `ago()` and `now()`, converters like `tostring()` and `toint()`, string helpers like `startswith`, `contains`, and `split`, and collection helpers like `make_set`, `make_list`, `array_length`, and `array_index_of`.

Just as important, the out-of-scope list is explicit. `mv-apply`, `evaluate bag_unpack`, `series_*`, parameterized user-defined functions, and external tables are not quietly half-implemented. They raise a clear error so the failure mode is "you hit an unsupported feature" instead of "you got a plausible-looking but wrong result."

sections.heading: The reproducibility trick that made the lab usable
paragraphs: One design detail matters more than it sounds: the module freezes the "current time" anchor when the context is created.

That means `ago()` and `now()` are reproducible against the static sample data. The browser lab and the PowerShell lab both depend on that idea. If the reference clock drifted with the user's system clock, training queries would keep getting weirder as the bundled data aged. Freezing the reference time lets the dataset stay static while the exercises still behave like they're running against a fresh window.
That small constraint is why the same query examples can be taught in the guide, graded in the practice harness, and validated in the browser engine without everyone getting different answers.

sections.heading: Why SQLite sits underneath it
paragraphs: SQLite is the storage layer, not the query language. The companion `Build-KqlLabDb.ps1` script stages CSV log samples into tables that match the production-style schema, and `Import-KqlLabCsv.ps1` handles the type coercion.
That split matters:

• SQLite gives me a portable local store. • PowerShell gives me a place to model KQL semantics directly. • The sample tables keep the field names and data shapes familiar enough that a hunt can move from the lab into Sentinel or ADX with minimal translation.
The browser lab later ports the same mental model into JavaScript and WASM SQLite, but the PowerShell version is the original reference implementation.

sections.heading: Where this fits in the rest of the site
paragraphs: `Invoke-KqlPS` is not an isolated script. It is the anchor point for a bigger chain:
• the local lab database builder • the KQL guide and examples • the browser playground • the 30-question practice harness • the validation matrix that keeps the browser port honest
That is the part I care about most. The goal was never just to write a parser. It was to build a practice environment where the query, the data, the lesson, and the grading path all line up.

If you want to poke at the browser side of the same idea, start with the [KQL Playground](/kql/) and [KQL Practice](/lab/practice/). If you want the PowerShell module inventory, the [Scripts page](/scripts/) is the map.

posts.title: MITRE Crosswalks in the Lab
posts.summary: How the local ATT&CK data, CVE-to-technique mappings, and KQL tooling fit together in one offline-friendly workflow.

sections.heading: The problem I wanted to solve
paragraphs: I did not want ATT&CK living in my tooling as a poster on the wall.

The useful version of ATT&CK is the one that can sit next to the things an analyst is already doing: checking whether a technique is relevant, seeing what data sources it expects, comparing it with recent CVEs, and turning that into a query or triage path without opening six tabs.
That is the job of the MITRE crosswalk pieces in this repo.

sections.heading: The local explorer starts with the full STIX bundle
paragraphs: `MitreAttackExplorer.ps1` downloads the Enterprise ATT&CK STIX bundle, parses it, and loads the useful pieces into the same SQLite database used by the rest of the SOC Dashboard tooling.
The ingest path stores:
• tactics • techniques and sub-techniques • intrusion sets • software • mitigations • relationships

The important design choice is that ATT&CK data is cached locally after the first run. That keeps the tool fast, user-level, and workable in environments where the interesting part of the day is analysis rather than waiting on a remote dependency.

For a while there was a browser version of the explorer on this site too. It shipped a slimmed static dataset so the public side stayed usable without a backend. I ended up pulling it down - the local dashboard explorer is where that work actually lives, and keeping two copies honest was more upkeep than it was worth.

sections.heading: CVE-to-ATT&CK mapping is intentionally a separate layer
paragraphs: The ATT&CK bundle alone answers "what is this technique?" It does not answer "which current vulnerabilities line up with the behavior I care about?"

That is why `Update-CveAttackMap.ps1` exists as a separate import step. It reads a CSV with `CveId` and `TechniqueId` columns, plus optional `Source`, `Confidence`, and `Mapping` fields, then loads those rows into the database as a first-class lookup table.
Separating the mapping layer from the ATT&CK ingest keeps a few good things true:

1. Multiple mapping sources can coexist. 2. Analyst-curated mappings are not flattened into someone else's feed. 3. The explorer and the patching views can show confidence and provenance, instead of pretending every mapping is equally authoritative.
The script header even calls out the intended mapping sources: the Center for Threat-Informed Defense mappings, NVD/CWE-derived bridges, and analyst-curated entries from local investigations.

sections.heading: Why this matters in practice
paragraphs: A local crosswalk turns three separate questions into one working loop:
• What technique is this adversary behavior pointing at? • What data source should see it? • Which current CVEs or products make that technique more urgent right now?
That is the connective tissue between the ATT&CK explorer, the CVE/KEV/EPSS browser, and the KQL tooling.

If a technique shows up repeatedly in ATT&CK-oriented research, and the related products are present in KEV with strong EPSS or ransomware linkage, that should change the order in which I write detections, validate log coverage, or bug a team about patching.
The repo already leans into that connection:

• the ATT&CK explorer keeps tactic / platform / relationship context close • the CVE browser already ships KEV and EPSS together • the KQL templates and practice surfaces provide a place to turn the framework view into an actual hunt

sections.heading: Why keep it offline-friendly
paragraphs: One theme across this site is that the interesting part should survive without a constant live dependency.

That is true for the KQL engine, and it is also true here. The ATT&CK bundle can be cached. The mapping import can be run on demand. The browser explorer can ship a trimmed JSON snapshot. That means the learning surface is still there even when the network is not.

I like that constraint because it forces the tooling to stay honest. If the tool only works when every external service is healthy, then the value is in the integration. If the tool still works offline, the value is in the model.

sections.heading: Where this goes next
paragraphs: The next useful step is not another page. It is tighter round-tripping:
• ATT&CK technique to starter KQL • CVE view to mapped techniques • templates tagged by ATT&CK technique • practice questions that say what tactic they are really exercising
That is the direction I want the lab to keep moving: less taxonomy for its own sake, more direct paths from framework language to an analyst doing the work.
If you want to poke at the live surfaces, start with the [Browser Lab](/lab/).

stories.title: Microsoft warns of high-volume phishing using fake Microsoft 365 service-health outage notices
stories.what: Microsoft Threat Intelligence says it observed a coordinated, high-volume phishing campaign on 13 November 2026 that targeted organizations across multiple sectors worldwide with emails posing as Microsoft 365 service-health notifications. The lures claimed messages had been held during an Exchange Online disruption and would be deleted within 24 hours unless the recipient clicked a link. According to Microsoft, the emails used subjects of the form "Outage – <random token>", display names made of a three-letter prefix plus "Outage Notification" or "Service Health", recipient-specific tracking links and a common…
stories.why: Any Microsoft 365 tenant is a plausible target, and randomized subjects and per-recipient links are designed to defeat simple pattern blocking. If users entered credentials, Microsoft flags risks of mailbox access, business email compromise, internal phishing and inbox-rule manipulation, so clicks since 13 November 2026 should be triaged now. Microsoft says Defender for Office 365 blocks and quarantines these…
actions: Search mail telemetry for messages since 13 November 2026 with subjects starting "Outage –" and sender display names ending in "Outage Notification" or "Service Health", and purge any delivered copies.
Identify users who clicked links in those messages, reset their passwords, revoke sessions and refresh tokens, and review their sign-in logs for unfamiliar IPs or devices.
Review mailbox rules and forwarding settings created after the click for affected users, removing rules that delete, move or forward mail.
Warn users that Microsoft does not send held-mail deletion notices of this kind and that real service-health status is shown in the admin center.

stories.title: ScreenConnect CVE-2026-84869 exploited in the wild against MSP technicians
stories.what: Huntress reports confirmed exploitation of CVE-2026-84869 in ConnectWise ScreenConnect, with attackers using it to run malicious files through the accounts of managed service provider technicians. The flaw is rated CVSS 9.9 (critical) and is listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The sources reviewed do not give affected or fixed version numbers, technical root cause, or the specific indicators Huntress published.
stories.why: ScreenConnect gives remote, high-privilege access to every endpoint it manages. A compromised MSP technician session can push and run files across many customer Windows servers and workstations at once. Exploitation is confirmed and the CVE is in CISA KEV, although no KEV due date is listed. EPSS is 1.2% and no public proof-of-concept is reported, but active exploitation should take priority over those scores.
actions: Identify every ScreenConnect server and client in your estate and at your MSPs, then apply the ConnectWise fix for CVE-2026-84869 as soon as ConnectWise confirms the patched version.
Ask your MSP whether its ScreenConnect instance is patched and whether it has reviewed technician accounts and sessions for misuse.
Hunt for files dropped and processes launched by ScreenConnect client services, especially script interpreters and newly written executables.
Review ScreenConnect technician accounts, enforce MFA, and rotate credentials for any account showing unexpected sessions or file transfers.

stories.title: Barracuda attributes November cloud breach to stolen cloud access key and ARTEX AI pentest framework
stories.what: BleepingComputer reported on 16 November 2026 that Barracuda has linked a breach of its cloud environment, which happened earlier in November, to attackers using a stolen cloud access key. According to the report, the intruders also used ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing framework. The available reporting does not say which Barracuda products or customer data were affected, how the key was stolen, or what the attackers did once inside.
stories.why: Barracuda sells email and network security products, and many of them connect to Microsoft 365 tenants through app consents, API tokens or connector credentials. Any customer data or integration secrets held in Barracuda's cloud could be misused. The sources do not confirm customer impact, so treat this as a supply-chain exposure check until Barracuda publishes details, not as a confirmed compromise of your tenant.
actions: Watch for Barracuda customer notifications and advisories about this incident, and follow any credential rotation guidance they issue.
Inventory Barracuda integrations with Microsoft 365 and Entra ID, including enterprise apps, service principals, API keys and mail connectors, and confirm each one is still needed.
As a precaution, rotate secrets and API tokens shared with Barracuda cloud services, and review the permissions granted to Barracuda apps in Entra ID.
Review recent activity by Barracuda-related apps and service principals in M365 audit logs and look for unusual mailbox access, configuration changes or new connectors.

stories.title: Unit 42 reports espionage campaign using PerfectPioneer RAT and KUKURAT with HTTP/3 C2
stories.what: Unit 42 published research on 16 November 2026 describing a cyberespionage campaign against government organizations in Southeast Asia. According to Unit 42, the operators deploy a remote access trojan it calls PerfectPioneer RAT and a modular implant called KUKURAT, and both use command-and-control channels built on HTTP/3, which runs over QUIC. The available summary does not include initial access vectors, attribution, targeted platforms or indicators of compromise.
stories.why: HTTP/3 C2 travels over UDP 443 as QUIC, which many proxies and TLS inspection stacks do not decrypt or log as well as HTTPS over TCP, so this traffic can slip past controls built for TCP. Government and public-sector defenders, especially those with Southeast Asian operations, should check whether non-browser processes are making QUIC connections. No CVE is involved, so there is nothing to patch; the defenses are…
actions: Review the full Unit 42 report and import any published indicators into Defender XDR custom indicators and Sentinel threat intelligence.
Hunt for non-browser processes that make outbound UDP 443 (QUIC) connections, especially from unsigned binaries or binaries in user-writable paths.
Where business needs allow, block outbound UDP 443 at the perimeter so clients fall back to TCP HTTPS, which proxies and inspection tools can see.
Make sure firewall and proxy logs capture UDP 443 flows with destination and byte counts, and send them to Sentinel.

explainer.concept: HTTP/3 and QUIC as a command-and-control channel
explainer.dek: QUIC is an encrypted transport that runs over UDP and carries HTTP/3; malware that uses it for command and control can slip past network controls built to inspect TCP-based HTTPS.
takeaways: Find out whether your firewall or secure web gateway decrypts, partially inspects, or simply passes QUIC on UDP 443, and record the answer for your current version.
Block outbound UDP 443 by default and allow it only to required destinations, so browsers fall back to inspectable TCP HTTPS; set the Chrome and Edge policies that disable QUIC to match.
Hunt in Defender XDR for outbound UDP connections to remote port 443 from processes other than approved browsers and known QUIC clients, prioritizing servers and unsigned or user-writable binaries.
Add UDP 443 flows to beaconing analysis in Sentinel, looking for regular intervals to rare external destinations contacted by only a few hosts.

stories.title: Cyrus SASL through 2.1.28: SRP mechanism flaw lets unauthenticated clients log in as any user
stories.what: NVD published CVE-2026-129483 (CVSS 9.3) on 15 November 2026. It describes an authentication bypass in the SRP server mechanism of Cyrus SASL through 2.1.28. The server-side SRP step does not validate the client's public value properly, so an unauthenticated network client can force a predictable shared secret. That lets the client authenticate as any existing user without the password and learn the session keys. NVD does not list affected vendor products or a fixed release.
stories.why: Cyrus SASL is embedded in many Linux mail, directory and IMAP services, and a successful bypass gives full account impersonation on whatever service uses it. Only deployments that offer the SRP mechanism should be exposed, so whether SRP is enabled decides real risk. There is no known exploitation, no public proof of concept, no KEV listing and an EPSS of 0.38%, so this is a prompt-patch and configuration review…
actions: Inventory Linux servers carrying Cyrus SASL (cyrus-sasl, libsasl2 packages), with internet-facing mail, LDAP and IMAP servers first.
Check whether the SRP mechanism plugin is installed and offered by each service. Where it is, remove the SRP plugin package or restrict the service's SASL mechanism list to exclude SRP.
Watch distribution and upstream Cyrus SASL advisories for a fixed release and apply it once available. The sources do not state a fixed version.

Review authentication logs of SASL-using services for successful SRP logins, especially from unexpected sources or for privileged accounts, and rotate credentials and session secrets if any look suspicious.

Forward SASL authentication logs to Sentinel and alert on any SRP-mechanism authentication, prioritising successful logins for administrative and service accounts.

stories.title: Huntress: Teams meeting-booking lure used to hide device code phishing
stories.what: Huntress reports that threat actors built a convincing Microsoft Teams meeting-booking flow to disguise device code phishing. The lure leads victims to complete a legitimate Microsoft device code sign-in, which authorizes the attacker's session and gives them access to the victim's account. stories.why: Device code phishing uses Microsoft's real sign-in pages, so URL reputation checks and user awareness of fake login pages often miss it. When it succeeds, the attacker receives tokens for the victim's Entra ID account, and MFA does not stop that. Huntress describes this as active use against victims. Any tenant that still allows the device code flow for ordinary users is exposed.
actions: Block the device code authentication flow with a Conditional Access authentication flows policy, and allow it only for named accounts or devices that need it, such as meeting room or kiosk devices.
Review Entra ID sign-in logs for recent device code authentications by users who do not normally use them, especially sign-ins from unfamiliar IPs or countries.
For any suspected compromised account, revoke sessions and refresh tokens, reset credentials, and check for new mailbox rules, MFA methods and device registrations.

stories.title: Microsoft: multiple threat actors deploy GSocket for persistent C2 on compromised Linux servers
stories.what: Microsoft reports several incidents in which threat actors installed GSocket, an open source remote access tool, on Linux servers after exploiting web application vulnerabilities. According to Microsoft, the tool let attackers keep access after the original vulnerabilities were patched. Defender for Endpoint telemetry shows the activity growing over recent months, concentrated on web applications and hosting environments. Microsoft notes that GSocket traffic goes through the public Global Socket Relay Network, so attackers need no infrastructure of their own.
stories.why: Patching an exploited web application does not evict an attacker who has already installed GSocket. Both ends connect outbound to a shared public relay, so there is no attacker-owned IP address or domain to block, and the host needs no inbound listener. Any Linux web or hosting server in your estate that was compromised and then only patched may still be under attacker control, and the sources describe exploitation…
actions: On any Linux web server with a past or suspected application compromise, check for GSocket binaries, processes and persistence before declaring the incident remediated.
Hunt for GSocket tool names (gs-netcat, gsocket, gs-sftp, gs-mount) in process and file telemetry across Linux devices onboarded to Defender for Endpoint.
Review cron jobs, systemd units, shell profile files and authorized_keys on affected hosts for persistence, and check for signs of privilege escalation.
Restrict outbound traffic from servers to the Global Socket Relay Network at the egress firewall or proxy, as Microsoft suggests, and alert on attempts to reach it.

stories.what: BleepingComputer reports that attackers are hosting their own instances of AntiFox, an open-source agentic penetration testing platform, on Alibaba Cloud infrastructure. According to the report, they use these instances to target web services and AWS environments in order to steal AWS credentials. The available reporting is brief. It does not name victims, specific vulnerabilities, indicators of compromise or the exact techniques the AI agents use.
stories.why: Agentic pentest tooling lets attackers automate reconnaissance and credential harvesting against internet-facing web applications at scale. Any public web service in your estate that holds or can reach AWS credentials is a potential target, including keys stored in config files, environment variables or instance metadata. Exploitation is confirmed in the wild, but no indicators have been published, so defenders…
actions: Inventory internet-facing web applications that store AWS access keys, or can retrieve them from environment variables, config files or instance metadata. Move them to short-lived role credentials where possible.
Enforce IMDSv2 on AWS EC2 instances so that server-side request forgery from a web app cannot easily read role credentials.
Review AWS CloudTrail and Defender for Cloud Apps for access key use from unfamiliar cloud provider IP ranges, including Alibaba Cloud. Rotate any keys used unexpectedly.
Look in web server and WAF logs for high-volume automated scanning that probes for exposed secrets such as .env files, configuration backups and cloud credential files.

Enforce SMB signing, LDAP signing and channel binding, and Extended Protection for Authentication to reduce NTLM relay risk.

stories.title: Huntress details four evolving ClickFix attack chains, including lateral movement and PNG-hidden payloads
stories.what: Huntress reports that ClickFix, a social engineering technique that tricks users into pasting and running attacker-supplied commands, has evolved. According to Huntress, recent chains add lateral movement, payloads hidden inside PNG image files, Node.js-based remote access trojans, and a browser cache abuse technique. The available summary does not give indicators, specific malware families, or victim details.
stories.why: ClickFix gets around many email and download controls because the user runs the command themselves, usually through the Windows Run dialog or a terminal, so any Windows endpoint with a human user is exposed. Huntress says the activity now goes beyond a single host to lateral movement, which raises the impact of one successful lure. No CVE or patch applies, so detection and user controls are the main defenses.
actions: Hunt for Run dialog (RunMRU) entries and explorer.exe-spawned shells that contain PowerShell, mshta, curl or encoded commands, and investigate any hits.
Hunt for node.exe running from user-writable paths such as AppData or Temp and making outbound connections, which may indicate a Node.js RAT.

Where business needs allow, restrict the Win+R Run dialog for standard users through Group Policy and enable Attack Surface Reduction rules that block obfuscated scripts and Office or script child processes.
After any confirmed ClickFix execution, check for lateral movement from the affected host and rotate the user's credentials.

According to the report, the attacker used that trusted access to reach the AWS environments of several Qubole customers and exfiltrate data from them. stories.why: Third-party SaaS platforms such as Qubole usually get cross-account IAM roles or access keys with broad read access to customer S3 data. actions: Inventory every IAM role, trust policy and access key that grants Qubole or other third-party platforms access to your AWS accounts. Revoke or suspend that access if it is not actively needed.

Reduce vendor role permissions to the specific buckets and actions the integration needs, and turn on S3 data events and GuardDuty for exfiltration anomalies.

templates.name: Critical Process Cloning
templates.description: Detects critical Windows processes (lsass, csrss, winlogon, svchost, services, wininit, smss) that appear as their own parent (Image == ParentImage) in Sysmon Event ID 1 - a hallmark of process-hollowing or impersonation.
templates.kql:
let CriticalProcesses = dynamic
([
    "lsass.exe"   , "csrss.exe"  , "winlogon.exe", "svchost.exe",
    "services.exe", "wininit.exe", "smss.exe"
]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EventID     == 1 
    and EventSourceName == 'Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon'
| extend CleanXml   = replace_string(EventData, @' xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/win/2004/08/events/event"', "")
| extend ParsedXml  = parse_xml(CleanXml)
| extend DataFields = ParsedXml.EventData.Data
| mv-apply Field=DataFields on (
    extend Key = tostring(Field['@Name']), Value = Field['#text']
    | summarize UnpackedData = make_bag(bag_pack(Key, Value))
)
| evaluate bag_unpack(UnpackedData, "Left_")
| extend
    ImageName       = tolower(tostring(split(Left_Image, "\\")[-1])),
    ParentImageName = tolower(tostring(split(Left_ParentImage, "\\")[-1]))
| where ImageName  == ParentImageName
| where ImageNa

templates.name: Sysmon 255 Drop Counter

templates.kql:
let Hostname  = "";
let startTime = datetime(2026-04-1);
let endTime   = datetime(2026-04-30);
//
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated between (startTime .. endTime)
| where Computer has (Hostname)
| where EventSourceName == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon"

| parse EventData with *'Events dropped from driver queue: 'Description'</Data>'*
| where ID <> 'GetConfigurationOptions'
| project EventCreation, Description, ID
| extend EventTypeDropped = todynamic(replace_string(tostring(extract_all(@'(\w+:)', Description)), ':', '')),
